facts.title: Named for a dwarf planet
facts.text: Cerium was discovered in 1803 by the Swedish chemists Jöns Jacob Berzelius and Wilhelm Hisinger, and independently by Martin Heinrich Klaproth in Germany. They named it after Ceres, the largest object in the asteroid belt, which had itself been discovered just two years earlier in 1801. At the time Ceres was considered a new planet, so the element honored what was then the freshest discovery in the night sky.

facts.title: The most abundant rare earth
facts.text: Despite belonging to the group called the 'rare earth elements,' cerium is not actually rare at all. It makes up roughly 66 parts per million of Earth's crust, making it about as common as copper and more abundant than tin, lead, or cobalt. The 'rare' label is historical, dating from when these elements were genuinely difficult to separate from one another, not because they are scarce.

facts.title: A metal that can ignite from a scratch
facts.text: Pure cerium is so reactive that shavings or filings of it can catch fire spontaneously in air at room temperature, a property called pyrophoricity. If you scratch a piece of cerium with a knife, the freshly exposed metal can spark and burn. This is why cerium must be stored carefully, often under mineral oil or in an inert atmosphere.

facts.title: The spark in your lighter
facts.text: The 'flint' in disposable lighters and old-fashioned fire starters is not flint at all but ferrocerium, an alloy that is mostly cerium and iron. When you spin the little steel wheel, it shaves off tiny pyrophoric particles that ignite in air, producing the shower of sparks that lights the gas. This same mismatch-named material has been used in survival fire-starters for over a century.

facts.title: Two faces, two valences
facts.text: Cerium is unusual among the lanthanides because it readily switches between two oxidation states, Ce(III) and Ce(IV). This easy back-and-forth makes its compounds excellent catalysts, since they can grab and release oxygen on demand. Cerium(IV) is one of the few stable +4 ions among the rare earths, a quirk tied to the extra stability of its empty 4f electron shell.

facts.title: It cleans your car's exhaust
facts.text: Cerium oxide is a key ingredient in the three-way catalytic converters fitted to gasoline cars. It acts as an 'oxygen buffer,' storing oxygen when the exhaust is rich and releasing it when lean, which keeps the conversion of harmful gases running efficiently. This oxygen-storage trick relies directly on cerium flipping between its +3 and +4 states.

facts.title: The polish behind clear glass
facts.text: Finely powdered cerium oxide, often called 'jeweller's rouge' for glass, is the world's premier polishing compound for optical surfaces. It is used to finish precision lenses, mirrors, telescopes, and smartphone screens, working through a combination of mechanical abrasion and gentle chemistry with the glass surface. It largely replaced older iron-oxide polishes because it cuts faster and leaves a finer finish.

facts.title: A strange behavior under pressure
facts.text: Cerium has one of the most complex phase diagrams of any element, with several different crystal structures depending on temperature and pressure. Most dramatically, near room temperature it undergoes an isostructural transition where its volume collapses by about 15 percent under modest pressure, with no change in crystal symmetry. Physicists study this 'gamma-to-alpha' transition because it reveals how the element's 4f electrons can suddenly become more involved in bonding.

facts.title: Sunglasses and UV-blocking glass
facts.text: Adding cerium oxide to glass lets it absorb ultraviolet light while staying transparent to visible light. This makes cerium-doped glass valuable for protecting museum displays, television tubes, and eyewear from UV damage and yellowing. The same property helps shield sensitive contents from the fading effects of sunlight.

facts.title: Forged in dying stars
facts.text: Cerium, like most elements heavier than iron, is not made in ordinary stellar burning but in neutron-capture processes inside aging stars and stellar explosions. Much of the universe's cerium is built by the slow neutron-capture 's-process' in red giant stars, with additional amounts from the rapid 'r-process' linked to supernovae and neutron-star mergers. Astronomers can detect its spectral lines in stars and even in the spectra of distant cosmic objects.
